name: Umar Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a hybrid hatchback on the east side, parcels from the retail park in the morning and takeaway in the evening, all through apps. It's mostly new-build estates, so the roads are easy, but the house numbers make no sense and I still get lost, ten months in. Weekends I fix up used electric bikes in my brother's garage and sell them online. I like the mix, the driving clears my head and the bikes keep my hands busy.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI in all of that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I ask a chatbot to plan which app to log into and when, and it helps me price the bikes and write the listings. Last month it spotted that I was losing money on Tuesday lunchtimes, so I stopped doing them. I've got about eight months of money saved, a few thousand in shares and six bikes in stock, so I'm comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped but the tools are still useful. I'd post a short video about how I use a chatbot to price bikes. People like that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine either way. The driving keeps paying, the bikes keep growing. I'd probably just be a bit annoyed I put money in robot shares last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both: driving in the week, bikes at the weekend. I'd try to sell ten bikes a month instead of six. I'd keep my shares and maybe move a bit into something boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal, like any other week of driving and fixing bikes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time AI does save you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put more hours into the bikes. If the chatbot does my bike listings in five minutes instead of an hour, that's two more bikes a week. Small things add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything in this picture that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, apart from the car getting old. It's at 140,000 miles. If it dies, that's a few thousand out of savings.

steps.text: Keep the weekday parcel and takeaway driving on the east side

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to be flexible. Some jobs shrink, some grow, and the people who adapt do fine. I'd keep my tone practical online, not preachy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's mostly good for me. The bits AI takes over in my life are the bits I'd rather not do, like listings and accounts. The driving and the fixing are hands-on, so they last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let AI do all my bookkeeping and the bike shop's messages. I'd put more savings into the bike business, maybe rent a small unit instead of using my brother's garage. I'd still drive four days a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. I like it when the boring jobs disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says thinking tasks go first. Where does that hit your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Admin. The planning, the messages with buyers, the tax stuff. My hands still do the real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about driving less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if the bikes take off. Three days driving, three days bikes would be perfect. But I'd want a year of proof first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready now, because two years isn't long. I'd tell my friends from the depot to save and learn something. Online I'd post what I'm doing, step by step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think driving goes by 2031, and that's most of my income. The bikes might last a bit longer, but robots could fix bikes too by then. I'd be okay for a while, but I'd have to rethink everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut driving to three days and put everything into the bike business while there's time. I'd sell my older shares and buy into the companies making the delivery robots. I'd also learn how to repair the robots themselves, because someone has to at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, sliding to anxious. But I've got moves to make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots doing hands-on work by 2031. Does that reach the bike repairs too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, eventually. But a person who knows the customer and the area will still have an edge for a few years. I'd lean into that, local and trusted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're comfortable. What would make you uncomfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the bike business flopped and the driving went in the same year, I'd be thirty with my savings dropping. I'd keep a full year of money aside to stop that happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decent window, so start now and don't wait. I'd share the tools I use and tell people which courses are worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can build the bike business properly first. By 2034 I want the bikes to be my main income, not the driving. That's doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drive five days for two more years to build savings, then cut to three. I'd rent the unit in 2028 and maybe hire one helper. I'd also put some money into robot companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried. It feels like a starting gun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three extra years change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother Adam, maybe as a partner in the bike shop. He's a warehouse picker and his job will go before mine. We'd do better together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you take along?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to test things. Two years means betting everything, but five means I can try, fail and try again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if you start early, and I'd keep saying it. I'd make the point that adapting isn't about being clever, it's about starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's very comfortable for me. I'd be thirty-seven with a business, savings and shares. Honestly, the robots arriving might even help, if I own a few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep driving and growing bikes, invest steadily, learn whatever AI tools come along. By 2032 I'd stop driving and run the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is more time than I've ever planned for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots around 2039. Is that a long time for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it's a lifetime in business. My dad started his market stall with less time than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd keep doing what I'm doing, just with a ten-year plan written down. I'd ask the chatbot to help me write it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit the driving and maybe the bikes before I'd built enough. What would help is cheap business loans for small repair shops and short courses on fixing robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about side businesses. A lot of drivers have a side business, selling or fixing something, and that's where a lot of us will land.

headlineQuote: A lot of drivers have a side business, selling or fixing something, and that's where a lot of us will land.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old** driver on the east side with a weekend e-bike repair business.
He uses a **chatbot daily** for planning, pricing and listings.
He has **eight months saved**, some shares and bikes in stock.
He's **pragmatic** and sees AI as a tool, even buying robot shares.
He's calm in most pictures, **anxious** only when driving ends by 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because driving and bike repairs could go before the business is built.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap business loans** for small repair shops.
